title: How to Follow Up With Past Clients (Without a Boring Newsletter)
summary: Close anniversaries, birthdays and life events: a twelve-month past-client follow-up plan with scripts, no newsletter required.
body_markdown:
Ask an agent how they stay in touch with past clients and you usually get one of two answers. A monthly market newsletter. Or a long pause.


The newsletter is the more common answer and the less useful one. It gets sent to everyone, it says nothing about the person receiving it, and it is almost never the reason a past client picks up the phone two years later.


Here is what works better.


## Why the newsletter doesn't do the job


A newsletter is a broadcast. Broadcasts are efficient, which is the appeal, and impersonal, which is the problem.


Your past client already knows you sell houses. What they need is a reason to think of you as their agent rather than an agent. A mass email cannot do that, because by definition it was not written for them. Most agent newsletters sit somewhere between ignored and unsubscribed.


There is also a quieter cost. A newsletter feels like follow-up. You send it, you tick the box, and you never notice that you have not had an actual conversation with anyone on the list in eighteen months. It substitutes activity for contact.


None of which means kill the newsletter. It means do not let it be the whole plan.


## What past clients actually remember


Think about the transaction from their side. Buying or selling a house is one of the more stressful things most people do. You were there for it. That is an unusually strong starting position, and it decays slower than agents assume, but it does decay.


What they remember is specific: the inspection that nearly killed the deal, the neighbor who came over with a bottle of wine, the week they thought they would lose the house. What they do not remember is your Q3 market summary.


Follow-up works when it is built on those specifics. Which means the job is less about writing good emails and more about having written things down.


## The anchors worth using


You need occasions. Without them you sit staring at a blank message wondering whether "just checking in" sounds as hollow as it reads. It does.


**Close anniversary.** The single best one. You know the date, it is meaningful to them, and nobody else in their life is going to mention it. One year, then annually. "Three years today. Did you ever replace that water heater?"


**Birthdays.** Low effort, high warmth, and worth doing by text rather than an automated card.


**Life events you already know about.** A baby due, a kid starting school, a job change, a renovation they mentioned. These are the highest-value touches you have, and they are entirely dependent on having noted them somewhere.


**Something genuinely useful about their house.** Not a market report. What the house two doors down just sold for. A contractor recommendation for the thing they complained about. Property tax reassessment news for their specific area.


**The unplanned one.** You saw something that reminded you of them. Send it. These land better than anything scheduled, precisely because they could not have been scheduled.


## A twelve-month shape


For a past client, four to six real touches a year is plenty. More than that starts to feel like marketing.


A workable pattern:


-


Close anniversary, every year, individual message


-


Birthday, individual message


-


One or two useful, house-specific notes across the year


-


One unplanned touch when something reminds you of them


-


Plus whatever broadcast you send, which sits on top and does not count


Notice that most of these are one-to-one. That is deliberate. Five personal messages a year beat twelve newsletters by a wide margin.


## Scripts you can actually use


**Close anniversary, year one:** "One year in the house today. Hard to believe it was such a fight to get it. How's it feeling now that you've actually lived in it through a winter?"


**Close anniversary, later years:** "Four years today. I still think about that inspection. Everything holding up?"


**Useful and specific:** "The place on the corner of your street just went for \[figure\]. Thought you'd want to know what that does for your number. No agenda, just useful to have."


**Reconnecting after too long:** "I realized it's been ages. No reason for the message other than you came to mind. How's everything?"


Short. No ask. The referral does not come from asking, it comes from being the agent they have most recently spoken to.


## The part that actually breaks


Everything above is easy to agree with and hard to sustain, for one reason: it depends on remembering.


Close dates live in your transaction system, birthdays live in your head, and the fact that they were planning a loft conversion lives nowhere at all. Lead CRMs do not help much here, because they are built to move new leads toward a close, not to hold a few hundred finished relationships and tell you which ones are going cold.


So the fix is unglamorous. The dates need to be stored against the person. The details they tell you need to be written down at the time, in a sentence, not filed for later. And something needs to surface both without you going to look, because you will not go to look.


That is the specific gap Dex is built for: your past clients with their close dates, birthdays and the details that matter, and a nudge when someone has drifted further than you meant to let them. For the full past-client touch plan and how it fits with your sphere and referral partners, see[the real estate agent's guide to sphere, past clients and referral partners](https://getdex.com/guides/real-estate-networking/) .


## Where to start


-


Export your past clients with close dates attached.


-


Add birthdays where you know them. Ask where you don't, it is not a strange question.


-


Write one line per person about what you actually remember from the transaction.


-


Set the anniversary reminders once.


-


Send this week's batch. Five messages, none of them asking for anything.


The first year feels like it is doing nothing. Then people start calling you before they call anyone else.
